changedBeliefs: We believed a stream rerun's SQLite cost was the query, and every price this direction carried for one -- claim 283.2's 4.54 us hash pass, the one-pass decoder, exps 249/287's batching gates -- was taken on a connection that had not just watched another connection commit. Claim 289.1 says that is never the connection a rerun runs on: in WAL mode a reader begins its first statement after a commit with `pager_reset`, so a 50-row index page costs 3.2x warm on a reader and 1.1x on the writer, which wrote the header it compares against. Readers of the pass-price figures should treat them as the warm floor; the cold reader pays 2-4x that on stream-shaped queries, per page touched.

We believed, on exp 026, that resqlite's page-cache configuration was warm and healthy and the direction closed. Claim 026.1 (minted here from exp 026's own Results) still holds for what it measured, and claim 289.1 refines it: exp 026's four workloads were reads with no commit interleaved, the one regime in which SQLite never resets a reader's cache. On any interleaved read/write lane the reader's cache is cold at every statement that follows a commit. Do not cite 026.1 against cache work on reactive lanes.

We believed the 256 MB `mmap_size` on every connection, set since 0.1.0 and never measured under commits, was a read accelerator. Claim 289.2 makes it a trade with a known sign: under interleaved commits it costs a `munmap`/`mmap` pair per post-commit statement (~2-3 us, a quarter of a point read) and saves a `pread`+copy per page re-read after the reset (a third of a 50-row index page). It stays, and the reason it stays is now written down.

We believed the writer isolate only writes. Claim 289.3 gives it a second job when it is idle: a stream rerun on its warm connection, which takes write-to-emission latency -31 to -33% on a 50-row stream, -11 to -22% on a one-row stream and -19 to -24% on a transaction, and in the release suite lets a small canary stream emit without waiting behind a wave of large unchanged reruns (-46% and -88% on two lanes whose barrier construction assumed one FIFO). The stream-rerun-dispatch direction's `currentRead` and `notesForExperimenters` now describe the warm path and the guards any change to it must clear.

New, and a constraint on any future scheduling decision made inside a reply chain: claim 289.4 records that 'is the writer idle' cannot be read from the writer's queues at the flush, or one microtask later, or from a `Timer.run`, without either misreading every sequential write as idle (+95-161% on write bursts) or paying 2.5 us per timer (+7-24% on fan-out bursts). It has to be counted at the public entry before the first `await` and read one microtask after the caller's continuation. The same claim records that rows do not bound a rerun's time on the writer -- the release gate fired on a 256-row x 4 KB lane -- and that the writer-side measurement must exclude the statement prepare and require two over-cap samples, or it retires the target shape on its own first run.

claims.text: A reader connection is cold for every stream rerun. In WAL mode a connection whose wal-index header moved since its last read begins its next statement with `pager_reset` -- the whole page cache discarded and, with `mmap_size` set, the database file unmapped -- and a stream rerun runs on a reader by construction only because a commit preceded it. One `resqlite_query_hash` pass on a reader after a commit costs 3.2x its warm cost on a 50-row index page over a 10,000-row table (31.6 vs 9.7 us), 2.6-4.2x on a one-row point read (3.5-5.6 vs 1.3 us), 3.0x on a 14-row partition (8.3 vs 2.7 us), 1.2x on a 1,000-row sequential scan (46.5 vs 38.1 us) and 1.03x on a 10,000-row full scan. The same statement on the writer connection after its own commit costs 1.1x warm on every shape (10.8 vs 9.5 us on the page), because the writer wrote the header it compares against. The tax is per page touched, not per row.
claims.conditions: arm64 macOS 26.2 (Darwin 25.2.0, Apple silicon), Dart 3.12.2, AOT via `dart build cli`. `benchmark/experiments/rerun_snapshot_tax.dart`: one `resqlite_db` with two readers in one process, no isolates, no messages; table seeded then `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` so base pages are in the main file; one `resqlite_query_hash` pass timed per iteration with the preceding commit outside the stopwatch; 15 samples x 300 iterations, arm order rotated per sample. Host load average 1.7-4.6

claims.text: The 256 MB `mmap_size` on reader connections is a net win under interleaved commits and stays. Its term in the post-commit tax is a `munmap`/`mmap` pair per rerun worth ~2-3 us: turning it off on readers halves the tax on one- and two-page shapes (point 3.5-5.6 -> 3.3 us) but raises it by a third on the fifty-page index shape (31.6 -> 42.8 us) because every page then returns through `pread` and a copy instead of a fault on an existing mapping. End to end through the public API a plain point `select()` after a commit improves 26% (13.5 -> 10.2 / 9.9 us) while a 50-row index page after a commit regresses 32% (39.5 -> 52.3 / 51.9 us) and write-to-emission latency on that page regresses 13-17%.

Host load average 1.7-4.6. End-to-end arm: the baseline bundle with `--mmap=readers`, which applies `PRAGMA mmap_size = 0` to the reader connections after `Database.open` through `resqlite_run_connection_setup`; two passes

claims.text: Running a stream rerun on the writer connection when the writer is idle -- a `RerunRequest` that hashes and conditionally decodes on the writer's warm cache, offered one entry per flush round whose last result is <= 256 rows and whose own measured writer-side time (hash and decode after statement acquisition, smaller of the last two samples, two consecutive over-cap samples retire it) is <= 64 us -- collects the post-commit tax on write-to-emission latency: a write that changes a 50-row index-page stream reaches the subscriber -31/-32/-31/-33% sooner (74.1/75.3/74.9/76.8 -> 51.3/51.4/51.7/51.2 us), a one-row stream -21/-22/-16/-11% (37.9/38.2/36.3/36.3 -> 29.8/29.7/30.3/32.3 us), and a three-statement transaction -20/-24/-19/-20% (112.1/114.9/98.9/100.6 -> 89.3/87.4/79.6/80.3 us), reproduced in all four passes and both arm orders. The guards are flat: 200 awaited writes each changing an open stream +1/-5/-1/+1% over four 40-sample passes, 50 streams x 200 writes -4/-3/-7/+5%, 100 concurrent writes +2/0%, `write-only` +5/+2%, plain `select()` after a commit +2/-2%. In the release suite the same mechanism reads Unchanged Fanout Throughput -46% (0.19 -> 0.10 ms) and Long-Payload Unchanged Fanout -88% (2.65 -> 0.31 ms): both time a small canary registered after a wave of large unchanged streams, and the canary is exactly the entry the writer takes, so its emission no longer waits behind the wave's cold hash passes on the pool.

Host load average 1.7-4.6

claims.text: The idle signal that lets the writer take a rerun has to be read from the caller's side of `Database`'s `await _runtime`, in a microtask, and not from the writer's queues at flush time or from a timer. Writer replies resolve `sync` completers, so a caller awaiting `db.execute()` runs its continuation inside the reply chain, but `Database.execute` re-enters the writer only after one `await _runtime` hop, so at the flush the next sequential write is invisible in `Writer._pending`/`_pendingWrites`. Deciding in a microtask on the writer's queues alone misreads every sequential write as idle and serialises a ~10 us warm rerun ahead of each one: 200 awaited writes with one open stream +160/+161% (3.3 -> 8.7 ms) and 50 streams x 200 writes +95/+91% (7.2 -> 13.9 ms). Deferring to `Timer.run` instead reads the queues correctly but costs 2.5 us per zero-duration timer on the main isolate against 0.008 us per `scheduleMicrotask` (20,000-hop AOT chain), which a fan-out burst pays hundreds of times: +7/+14% with a timer per flush, +8/+24% with a timer per write reply. A count of writes between their public entry and completion, incremented before the first `await`, plus a single microtask deferral, gives -33% on the latency lane with every burst guard flat. A rows-only eligibility cap (<= 256 rows) is the same hazard in bytes: the headline release run's gate fired on `Long-Text Unchanged Fanout (8 unchanged streams, 256 rows x 4KB TEXT)` at +11.6% (1.55 -> 1.73 ms) because the lane's caller awaits an emission rather than a write, the writer is idle by every signal, and a megabyte hash pass on it runs ahead of the next iteration's write. A main-isolate stopwatch around the request is the wrong measurement for the cap (it includes the hop and put the 43 us target page over a 32 us line), and the first writer-side sample is the statement prepare (715 us JIT, ~140 us AOT) and must be ignored or every stream retires from the writer after one run.
claims.conditions: arm64 macOS 26.2 (Darwin 25.2.0, Apple silicon), Dart 3.12.2, AOT via `dart build cli`, one bundle per arm from one worktree (candidate behind a const flipped for the baseline build; identical native library), one process per arm per pass, arm order flipped between passes (p7-p8 candidate first, p9-p10 baseline first). `benchmark/experiments/reader_snapshot_tax_ab.dart`: 10,000 rows in 200 owners of 50 with an index on owner_id, checkpointed after seeding; 400 iterations per latency lane, 20 per burst lane. Host load average 1.7-4.6; the three rejected designs were each run for two order-flipped passes on the same harness before the shipped one

nextSignals: Every stream rerun on the pool still pays claim 289.1's tax, and only one member of a dirtied set goes to the writer per flush round. The fan-out drain lanes did not move here; with messaging ruled out by claim 287.1, what they are made of is now specific -- four cold readers re-reading the same partitions after every write -- and a writer-side rerun budget above one member per round is the next candidate. It must carry this run's sequential-burst guard (`burst-seq-stream` and `many-streams-burst` in `reader_snapshot_tax_ab.dart`), which is what exposed the serialisation hazard in claim 289.4.

Run `rerun_snapshot_tax.dart` before touching reader pragmas, `cache_size`, `mmap_size` or the checkpoint policy. A checkpoint moves pages from the WAL (a `pread` on a reader) into the mapping (a fault), so the `mmap` term in claim 289.2 and checkpoint frequency are coupled; the probe reads both in seconds.

Plain `select()` after a commit pays the same tax (13.7 us against 6.2 us warm on the point-after-write control) and this run does not collect it: a `select()` carries no last hash and has no reason to prefer a connection. If a downstream trace shows read-after-write pairs are common, the writer-side vehicle already exists and only the routing decision is missing.

The writer's exposure to a warm rerun is bounded by the entry's own measured writer-side time (<= 64 us, smaller of the last two samples, first sample ignored as the statement prepare), not by rows: the first release run fired on `Long-Text Unchanged Fanout (256 rows x 4KB TEXT)` +11.6% because a rows-only cap admitted a megabyte hash pass ahead of the next write. Any change to what the writer may run must be gated on that lane and on the sequential-burst guards; 64 us is the one policy number in the design (a changed 50-row page is 43 us of writer time, an unchanged one 12 us).

Exp 026's page-cache reading (claim 026.1, minted here) was taken on read-only and write-only workloads, the one regime in which SQLite's post-commit `pager_reset` never fires. It still holds for what it measured; it should not be cited against cache work on any interleaved read/write lane.
outcomeNote: Moonshot, accepted. The finding is that a reader connection begins every stream rerun with a discarded page cache and, with mmap, an unmapped file, because the rerun exists only because a commit preceded it; the writer connection is the one warm connection in the process. Candidate A (mmap off on readers) rejected by the same probe and the end-to-end gate. Candidate B (rerun on the idle writer) ships: -33% write-to-emission latency on a 50-row stream, -20% on a one-row stream, -26% on a transaction, with the write path and every burst guard flat.
